# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is the strongest evidence in the set. It adds a second, independent hours measure, registers the mediation test before outcomes were known, compares the counter arm with control, and corrects the meta-analysis using that review's own supplementary table. Its main finding, a smaller but real per-hour gain at two years, is credible. But three problems cut across its headline claims, and the report doesn't acknowledge any of them:

- **Control-arm contamination** after month 15 makes the measured decay larger than the true decay.
- **The "confirmatory" meetings test** uses the same offices that produced the hypothesis.
- **The log-based hours measure** probably excludes meetings, which changes what both the "stricter" per-hour figure and the mediation result mean.

## 1. The numbers check out, but the summary mixes measures

| Check | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuers' hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden continuers' per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Counter staffing need | 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) | ≈ +13%, close to "12%" ✓ |

The counter-arm costing is consistent with the nine-month figures. That is a good sign.

**But the Summary compares unlike measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% uses timesheets and the 8.5% uses logs. The body correctly says the like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, a decline of about 22%. Section 5's "about a quarter" roughly matches that, but the Summary's version implies about a third.

## 2. Contamination in the control arm makes the decline look larger

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings, and their output per hour rose by 4.1%. The report treats this only as an "unplanned observation" about reorganising without cutting hours. It doesn't note what it does to the main estimate.

If control output per hour rises, the treated-minus-control gap shrinks even if treated offices haven't changed. As a rough calculation, two of seven offices at +4.1% raises the control average by about 1.2 points. That could account for **close to half of the 2.7-point decline** between nine and 24 months. The true decay in the treated offices may be noticeably smaller than reported.

It also seems likely these offices cut meetings *because* the nine-month report had publicised the meetings finding. That makes it a spillover from the trial, not a coincidence.

Two analyses are needed:

- the 24-month estimate excluding those two offices, or a version that adjusts for their change, and
- the meeting-audit effect estimated against the **other five control offices**, which were available as a comparison group. The +4.1% is an uncontrolled before-after figure, open to seasonality and regression to the mean.

## 3. The "confirmatory" meetings test is not an independent replication

Registering the mediation test at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes, is good practice. But the test runs on **the same seven treated offices** whose month-six pattern produced the hypothesis. If the offices that cut meetings most at month six are still the ones with the biggest gains at month 24, the test will pass partly because the same pattern is still there.

"A larger sample of office-months" doesn't solve this. Office-months within an office aren't independent, so the effective sample is still about 14 clusters. **CIs of 28–66% look narrow for that**, and the report should say how clustering was handled.

There is a further causal problem. Treatment was randomised, but meeting cuts were not. Managers who cut meetings may also have improved other workflows, which would make both meetings and output look connected. The Limitations section mentions this assumption, but the Summary says the analysis "**confirms**" the pathway. "Is consistent with" would be accurate.

The finding is now **stronger** than Varga & Holm allowed. It is no longer only an exploratory correlation across seven offices. But it still needs testing in new organisations.

## 4. What do the system logs measure?

The logs record "time staff are working on cases" on the case-management system. That probably **excludes meetings**, as well as phone calls, paper work and other off-system tasks. If so:

- **The hours measures can't be compared directly.** Timesheets cover all work. Logs cover only time spent on cases. Treated offices cut about 3.5 hours of meetings a week, so case time would fall *less* than total time even if no unrecorded work existed. The 11% vs 12% gap may simply reflect time moved from meetings to cases, not hidden work. The original question about unrecorded hours isn't really answered.
- **The mediation outcome changes meaning.** Output per *case-hour* excludes meeting time from the denominator. So the meetings pathway can't be the mechanical effect of removing unproductive hours. It would have to work through fewer interruptions and more focus. That is a more interesting finding, but the report should say which mechanism it is claiming.
- Logs can also count idle time while logged in, and miss work done off the system.

## 5. Gaps carried over from the nine-month report

- **Cost per case** is still missing for case-processing, even though it is now estimated for the counter arm. Output per employee is −3.4% and timesheet hours suggest some overtime continues, so cost per case has probably risen.
- **Backlog and time-to-decision** are still not reported, despite being named as a nine-month concern.
- **Output per employee is trending down**, from −2.1% to −3.4%, and its CI now reaches −8%. "Mostly, not fully, offset" is accurate, but this loss is growing.
- **Quality** is again reported as end-of-trial levels (3.2% v 3.0%) rather than as a difference-in-differences.
- **Resignations** still have no CI.

## 6. Two data points can't establish a trend

Section 3 rightly rejects the Halden energy extrapolation, which predicted the gain would reach zero by month ten. But two time points, 9 and 24 months, can't distinguish a plateau from a continuing decline either. That is the same objection raised against Varga & Holm. The trial almost certainly has monthly output data. Showing the trajectory, including month 15 when the control contamination began, would settle the question far better than two points.

## 7. The Halden subset

- **Response bias.** 14 of 23 agreed to take part. The nine who didn't are probably weighted toward worse outcomes, so even the "upper bound" framing may be generous. The authors' "survivors twice over" caveat is otherwise exemplary.
- **One reversion doesn't fit the binary categories.** The report says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But a marketing agency is discretionary work under the meta-analysis definitions. Client deadlines are a different kind of constraint from staffing opening hours, and grouping them together after the fact makes the classification look neater than it is. This supports the meta-analysis's warning that the binary oversimplifies.
- **An omission given the authorship.** R. Okafor, lead author of the Halden working paper, is a co-author here. The report doesn't correct the misdescribed attrition that Varga & Holm documented, which was the clearest outright error in the literature.

## 8. Rebuttals of earlier claims

- **Against "entirely an artifact": convincing.** The 24-month Varden estimate meets every standard Varga & Holm set: records, an objective hours measure, randomisation and two years. It still excludes zero. Contamination in the control arm, if anything, biases it downward.
- **Against "no sign of decay": convincing.** If all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, the meta-analysis's duration claim falls. Readers should check the supplementary table, but the claim is specific and checkable.
- **Authorship.** The authors are evaluating their own earlier hypothesis and replying to critics of their own and their co-author's work. This doesn't make the findings wrong, but independent replication matters more as a result.

## 9. Fair summary

> In a randomised trial, case-processing offices on a reduced schedule still showed higher output per hour after two years. The gain was about 10% on timesheets and 8.5% on case-system time, down from 12.5% at nine months. Some of that decline is probably due to two control offices independently cutting meetings. Output per employee was about 3% below control and may be slipping, and cost per case is still not reported. Cuts to recurring meetings are the leading explanation for the gain, now supported by a registered test, but in the same offices that suggested the idea. Reduced fatigue played a smaller role. In coverage-bound work, the reduced schedule was abandoned because restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff.

## Updated picture across all five documents

| Question | Previous best answer | After this report |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain | 8–12% (discretionary, actual hours) | **About 8–10% at two years in the strongest study; a modest decline, partly due to control contamination** |
| Per-worker output | Flat to slightly down / −9 to −11% | **About −3% and possibly growing (discretionary); coverage arm abandoned, with an estimated +9% cost per contact to restore service** |
| Durable? | Unknown | **Mostly yes to two years in one employer; trend shape unknown** |
| Mechanism | Unknown; meetings the leading hypothesis | **Meetings is the largest measured pathway, fatigue smaller, about a third unexplained; needs testing elsewhere** |
| Reorganisation without cutting hours? | Not asked | **The key open question, which no study has tested** |

That last row is now the most important. If cutting meetings delivers a large share of the gain, the policy question shifts from "should we cut hours?" to whether cutting hours is what makes reorganisation happen and last. That calls for a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation alone, and control.
